title: The Prestige: Benchmarking Cognitive Visual Reasoning using Magic Tricks
claim: Even leading models, given a video containing deliberate misdirection, miss part of what makes it surprising, which shows a gap in visual reasoning.
layout: 3 stacked tiers: question and surprise cues on top, filmstrip in the middle, three model answers below
description: The figure is a top-to-bottom example of one benchmark item. The top banner is a blue chevron strip. On the left is a user icon with a speech bubble asking "Why people are surprised watching this video?" Below it is the label "Question type: Paradoxical reasoning". On the right, two photo cards are labeled "Smoke Emission" and "Vanishing Deck", each with a red exclamation mark. A timeline with timestamps sits under the banner and links the cards to specific moments. A black filmstrip below it holds seven frames of a magician handling a Bicycle card box, and smoke appears in the later frames. The bottom row has three response cards, one each for Gemini, Qwen and ChatGPT. Each card shows a response time, an icon (green check or yellow warning), excerpted text with key phrases in red, and a verdict footer: "BOTH surprises identified!" or "Missing ONE surprise...". The red phrases and the filmstrip draw the eye first.
caption: An example prompt to challenge representative VLMs to explain the elements of surprise in a video sequence. Results highlight current limitations in VLM visual reasoning. All models are evaluated using their latest web versions at the time of testing. Responses are excerpted, and images are cropped for brevity. Project page
abstract: We introduce The Prestige, a video understanding benchmark that probes cognitive visual reasoning through professional magic performances, where deliberate misdirection challenges models to track events and explain unexpected outcomes. The benchmark comprises open-ended questions ranging from temporal and causal understanding to robustness against adversarial questions. Evaluation of leading open-source and proprietary VLMs reveals a substantial gap between even the strongest model and human performance. We also find systematic discrepancies between human and automated grading and identify recurring model failure modes. Ablations further show that models can select correct multiple-choice answers even when they fail to generate correct explanations independently, motivating further investigations into question formats. Together, these findings highlight limitations in both VLM reasoning and its evaluation, underscoring the need for more reliable video understanding models and more rigorous benchmarks.
